newsitem.title: ITALY: Former Italian soldier lied over Somalia killings.
newsitem.headline: Former Italian soldier lied over Somalia killings.

text.p: A former Italian soldier who alleged that troops on a United Nations mission to Somalia had killed unarmed civilians has admitted he lied, a prosecutor said on Thursday.

Biaggio Insacco, a public prosecutor in the Sicilian capital Palermo, told a news conference that ex-fusilier Benedetto Bertini had admitted fabricating evidence published last Friday in the weekly news magazine Panorama.

"I invented everything for the money," Insacco quoted Bertini as telling investigators. "Those dead Somalis shown in the photos had actually been blown up by a mine, they weren't killed by Italian paras."
Panorama published photographs which showed the scene of the death of at least six civilian Somalis.
Bertini claimed in a Panorama interview that they had been killed in 1993 when their jeep was hit by rifle grenades fired by Italian paratroops "for fun".

The story formed part of a Panorama expose of the alleged torture, rape and gratuitous killing of Somalis by Italian troops in Somalia from late 1992 to early 1994 as part of the U.N.'s multinational military mission.
The allegations caused deep shock in Italy, a former colonial power in Somalia, and have led to four separate investigations, including one called by the government.
Bertini retracted his allegations after failing to deliver to a Panorama journalist more photographs of alleged atrocities which he had promised to hand over on Wednesday night.

He instead entered a hospital in Palermo claiming he had been stabbed while on his way to the meeting but later said he invented the assault to try to hide the fact that he did not have the photographs, police said.
Panorama said on Thursday it had been wrong to publish Bertini's allegations but would stand by other reports of troop misconduct in Somalia.
Two generals who led Italian troops in Somalia resigned last weekend in a step they said would ease and speed up investigations over the alleged abuses.
Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta, reacting to Bertini's retraction, said many of the accusations had little basis but that investigations would continue while any doubt remained.
"The problem is serious and as long as there is the slightest suspicion of the armed forces we will carry on our investigations," Andreatta told reporters.
